newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Bluem ready for pension compromise - paper.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Bluem ready for pension compromise - paper.

text.p: German Labour Minister Norbert Bluem said on Monday that Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition government might be willing to back off from plans to lower Germany's pension payments.

"If the (opposition) Social Democrats have other ideas by which to reduce the burdens on those paying contributions, then we would be ready to discuss cuts in the pension payments," Bluem told German mass circulation daily Bild.

Bluem however warned that any potential savings would need to be real savings rather than a shifting around of costs, adding that the SPD's previous suggestions, which would hurt taxpayers, would not be sufficient.

Bluem has proposed modest reductions in pensions to cope with the "greying" of Germany and has won government approval for a plan which would eventually reduce a typical pension to 64 percent of average net wages -- a level last seen in the 1970s -- from around 70 percent now.

At the same time, the transfer of around 15 billion marks ($8.7 billion) in non-welfare costs from the state pension fund to the federal budget would enable contributions to be cut from today's record level of 20.3 percent of wages.
The SPD has sharply criticised the proposals and has threatened to turn the issue into a key campaign topic as preparations for the 1998 federal election begin in earnest.
